For afterward these things first began to be inquired into in this city by Socrates, then were brought down to this place; nor was it doubted that in virtue all hope both of living well and likewise happily was placed. Which things when Zeno had learned from our school, as is wont to be prescribed in legal actions, he \"did the same thing in another manner.\" This you now approve in him. Forsooth, the names of things being changed, he escapes the charge of inconstancy; we cannot escape it! He says the life of Metellus is not happier than that of Regulus, yet to be preferred — not more to be sought, but more to be taken; and, if there were a choice, the life of Metellus to be chosen, that of Regulus to be rejected; I call that life, which he says is to be preferred and more to be chosen, the happier, nor do I assign by any least weight more to that life than the Stoics.

89. What is the difference, except that I call known things by known words, while they seek new names by which to say the same? So, as in the senate there is always someone who demands an interpreter, so those men must be heard by us with an interpreter. I call good whatever is according to nature, what is contrary, evil; and not I alone, but you too, Chrysippus, in the forum, at home; in the school you cease. What then? Do you think men ought to speak one way, philosophers another? How much each thing is worth, the learned and the unlearned say differently; but when it has been agreed among the learned how much each thing is worth — if they were men, they would speak in the customary way — provided the things remain, let them coin words at their discretion.

90. But I come to the charge of inconstancy, lest you say too often that I stray; which you place in words, I thought it placed in the thing. If this be sufficiently perceived — in which we have the Stoics as the best of helpers — that there is so great a force of virtue that all things, if they be placed on the other side, do not even appear, when all the things which they at least call advantages, and to be taken and to be chosen and preferred — which they so define that they are to be valued at a fairly great worth — these things, then, when I call them by so many names used by the Stoics, partly new and invented, like those \"brought forward\" and \"reduced,\" partly signifying the same — for what is the difference, whether you seek or choose? to me indeed that which is chosen, and to which choice is applied, seems even more elegant — but when I have called all those things goods, it matters only how great I say they are, when things to be sought, how strongly. But if I neither call them more to be sought than you to be chosen, nor value them at more, I who call them goods, than you who call them \"brought forward,\" all those things must necessarily be darkened and not appear and run, as it were, into the rays of virtue as into those of the sun.

91. But, you say, that life in which there is something of evil cannot be happy. Then neither is a cornfield happy with rich and thick ears, if you see oats anywhere; nor merchandise profitable, if amid the greatest gains it has contracted a little loss. Or is this so everywhere, and otherwise in life? And will you not judge of the whole from the greatest part? Or is it doubtful that virtue so holds the greatest part in human affairs that it overwhelms the rest? I shall dare, then, to call the other things which are according to nature goods, and not to cheat them of their old name, nor now to seek out some new one rather, but to place the greatness of virtue, as it were, in the other scale of the balance.

92. That scale, believe me, will press down both earth and seas. For always from that which contains the greatest parts and pours itself out most widely the whole thing is named. We say that someone lives cheerfully; if, then, he has once been made rather sad, is the cheerful life lost? But this did not happen in that Marcus Crassus, whom Lucilius says laughed but once in his life, that on that account he was called less 'unlaughing,' as the same man says. Polycrates of Samos they called happy. Nothing had happened to him which he did not wish, except that he had thrown into the sea a ring in which he delighted. Was he, then, unhappy by that one annoyance, and happy again, when that very ring was found in the entrails of a fish? But he indeed, if he was foolish — which certainly, since he was a tyrant — was never happy; if wise, not even then was he wretched, when he was driven onto the cross by Oroetes, the satrap of Darius. 'But he was afflicted with many evils.' Who denies it? But those evils were overwhelmed by the greatness of virtue.

93. Or do you not grant even this to the Peripatetics, that they may say that the life of all good men — that is, of the wise and adorned with all the virtues — always has, in all its parts, more of good than of evil? Who says this? The Stoics, of course. By no means; but those very men who measure all things by pleasure and pain — do they not cry that the wise man always has present more of what he wishes than of what he does not wish? Since, then, those men place so much in virtue, who confess that for virtue's sake, unless it produced pleasure, they would not turn even a hand, what ought we to do, who say that even the least pre-eminence of mind goes before all the goods of the body, so that they are not even left in sight? For who is there who would dare to say that this falls within the wise man — that, if it could be, he would cast away virtue forever, to be freed from all pain? Who of us would say — we whom it does not shame to call those things which the Stoics call harsh, evils — that it is better to do something basely with pleasure than honourably with pain?

94. To us that Dionysius of Heraclea seems shamefully to have deserted the Stoics on account of pain of the eyes. As though, forsooth, he had learned this from Zeno — not to be in pain when he was in pain! He had heard, but had not learned, that that was not an evil, because it was not base, and was to be borne by a man. Had he been a Peripatetic, he would have remained, I believe, in his opinion — those who say pain is an evil, but, about bearing its harshness bravely, give the same precepts as the Stoics. And indeed your Arcesilas, although he was rather obstinate in arguing, yet was ours; for he was of Polemo's school. He, when he was burning with the pains of the gout, and his very intimate friend Charmides the Epicurean had visited him and was going out sad, said: 'Stay, I pray, our Charmides; nothing comes from there to here.' He showed his feet and his breast. And yet he would have preferred not to be in pain.

95. This, then, is our reasoning, which seems to you inconstant: that, on account of a certain heavenly and divine and so great pre-eminence of virtue, that, where virtue is, and great things and supremely praiseworthy done by virtue, there wretchedness and tribulation cannot be — yet toil can be, annoyance can be — I do not hesitate to say that all the wise are always happy, but yet that it can come about that one be happier than another.' 'And yet that point, Piso,' said I, 'must be confirmed by you again and again; which if you hold, you may lead away not only my Cicero, but even me myself.'

96. Then Quintus: 'To me indeed,' said he, 'this seems sufficiently confirmed, and I rejoice that that philosophy, whose furniture I formerly valued more than the possessions of the rest — so rich did it seem to me, that I could seek from it whatever I had desired in our studies — this philosophy, then, I rejoice has been found even more acute than the rest, which some said was lacking to it.' 'Not more, indeed, than ours,' said Pomponius, jesting; 'but, by Hercules, your discourse was most pleasing to me. For the things which I thought could not be said in Latin, those have been said by you in fitting words, and no less plainly than they are said by the Greeks. But it is time, if you please, and indeed straight to my house.' When he had said this, and it seemed to have been discussed enough, we all proceeded into the town, to the house of Pomponius.
